name: Wholecut shoes

lead: A wholecut shoe has its upper made from one piece of leather, with a single seam at the back or sometimes none. The unbroken surface reads as sleek and formal, and is a common choice for tailoring and dressier outfits.

The appearance payoff is styling: a smooth, uninterrupted vamp can make the foot look longer and more refined, and polished leather signals care for presentation. It is a style choice rather than a technique with studies behind it.

paras: They are worn as formal Oxfords or similar dress shoes with suits and smart outfits, and kept looking sharp by polishing and shoe trees. Leather and colour (black, brown, burgundy) set the formality.
Shoe fit and break-in vary; leather soles are less grippy in wet weather. Single-piece construction needs good hide, which is reflected in price.

angle.text: Wholecut shoes change how an outfit reads by providing a smooth, formal silhouette. They are a clothing choice used to dress up tailoring.

lead: A wholecut shoe, most often a wholecut Oxford, has an upper cut from a single piece of leather, with one seam at the back or, rarely, none.[1] Oxfords themselves are lace-up shoes with closed lacing, where the eyestays sit under the vamp, a design generally regarded as more formal than open-laced derbies.[1]
People wear wholecut shoes as a way to look polished: the clean, seam-free line is associated with formal tailoring. The shoe is a style item and has no clinical research attached.
infobox: Upper from one piece of leather

paras: Common Oxford variants include cap-toe, plain-toe, brogue and whole-cut styles; whole-cut distinguishes itself by lacking a toe cap or panels.[1]

The origin of the Oxford is uncertain. One account links it to Oxford University students shortening knee-high boots; another credits Prince Albert and Balmoral Castle. It evolved from the Oxonian half-boot around 1800 and reached North America in the 1800s, though the source flags these claims as needing more citations.[1]

timeline.event: The Oxonian half-boot, ancestor of the Oxford, is popular at Oxford.[1]
